By
NITIN NOHRIA

I once had the pleasure of visiting the historian
Doris Kearns Goodwin
at her home in Massachusetts. I wasn’t surprised to find her home filled with books, but one particular bookshelf did surprise me. It ran the whole length of a library wall and contained nearly 500 books.
Each one was a biography of Abraham Lincoln.
Lincoln is, of course, a giant historical figure who is worthy of study and admiration, and I’m especially fond of “Team of Rivals,” Ms. Goodwin’s masterly look at how Lincoln built his leadership team.
But as I’ve reflected on her vast library of Lincoln histories, I’ve wondered whether society might benefit if authors, filmmakers and the public paid as much attention to the history being made by business leaders.
I thought about Ms. Goodwin’s Lincoln library a few nights ago while watching the new film “
Steve Jobs
.” Mr. Jobs was a once-in-a-generation business leader, and while one can applaud or criticize his portrayal in the new Aaron Sorkin and Danny Boyle film, or the recent Alex Gibney documentary “Steve Jobs: The Man in the Machine,” or the other releases that preceded them, in my view it’s a positive thing for the public to be considering his legacy.
In fact, if more C.E.O.s were subject to this sort of retrospective assessment, they might manage differently.
Consider how rare it has become to read a first-rate biography of a corporate C.E.O. I’m not talking about an autobiography or memoir, such as Andy Grove’s “Only the Paranoid Survive” (one of my favorites), but a truly objective, deeply reported work that counts as legitimate history.
Walter Isaacson’s biography of Mr. Jobs, which was the basis for Mr. Sorkin’s script, is the kind of book I have in mind. Although Mr. Sorkin’s film takes significant liberties with real-life events, I admired the film’s effort to capture both the complexities of Mr. Jobs’s personality and the relationship between his professional and private lives.
There are very few books like this written, and I think it has an effect on the way business leaders manage their enterprises. Most observers attribute a chief executive’s short-term orientation to the pressures of capital markets or the lure of market-based incentive compensation, and I agree these are powerful forces.
But there are also quieter, inner-directed, psychological forces that play a role in C.E.O.s’ managerial myopia. I believe the outside world’s limited interest in making long-term evaluations of business leaders’ legacies is one factor that leads them to prioritize the here and now over the long term.
Like political leaders, every business leader thinks about — and should think about — his or her legacy. Legacies aren’t snap judgments. They’re the long-term, considered reconciliation of a leader’s accomplishments and failings.
In politics, leaders take great solace in this long-term sorting-out, a process that often results in profound reversals. Presidents who are initially judged as middling, or worse, often see their reputations burnished in the fullness of time. Harry S. Truman is perhaps the most notable example of this; George H. W. Bush is a recent example whose reconsideration is developing. George W. Bush has frequently referred to this phenomenon. History will be the ultimate judge of his administration’s decisions, he told CNN in 2013. “I’m just not going to be around to see the final verdict. In other words, I’ll be dead.”

Business leaders can take no such comfort, because in their world this re-examination rarely happens. Once they leave office, even the best-known business leaders are quickly forgotten. Last year in my commencement address, I had planned to refer to Lee Iacocca, who wrote a best-selling memoir of the turnaround he led at Chrysler in the early 1980s. My staff talked me out of it: They argued that today, more than 20 years after his retirement, many M.B.A. students may have no idea who Mr. Iacocca is.
It’s a reminder that in business, unlike in political or national histories, even monumental achievements can be quickly forgotten. Most business schools offer few (if any) courses in business history. (Harvard Business School has such a course, but it’s an elective instead of a core requirement.) Today many of the brightest M.B.A.s may know little of Thomas Watson or even Andrew Carnegie.
Against this backdrop, it’s only natural for business leaders to want to manage in a way that allows them to enjoy the fruits of their efforts during their time in the job — and to make decisions that cause the company to be successful now, while they’re leading it, instead of tomorrow, when hardly anyone will remember that they led it.
Perhaps this is no surprise. The creative destruction described by the economist Joseph Schumpeter is a powerful force. Great companies come and go, and the people leading them may seem even more ephemeral.
But I worry that we’re too quick to forget the accomplishments of great business leaders, and that if the people leading companies felt some solace that their long-term legacies might warrant a more careful evaluation, as is now occurring around Steve Jobs, they might make very different decisions.

Midway through “The Diver’s Clothes Lie Empty,” Vendela Vida’s nameless protagonist finds herself sitting in a private V.I.P. lounge in the Regency Hotel in Casablanca. She is chatting with the personal bodyguard of an American movie star. The bodyguard describes his interest in the evolutionary theory of “punctuated equilibrium,” in which species, faced with a dramatic change in their circumstances, adapt rapidly. The young woman, who is being vetted for the part of stand-in to the famous actress in a film being shot in Casablanca, feigns amiable curiosity. She is desperate to appear sufficiently sane and normal to get the job; she doesn’t want the bodyguard to realize that she herself is living proof of “punctuated equilibrium,” that the sequence of events that have occurred in the 48 hours since her arrival in Casablanca have propelled this previously unremarkable woman into committing a series of frauds that could get her into an awful lot of trouble.
“The Diver’s Clothes Lie Empty” (its title comes from a Rumi poem) is Vida’s fourth novel. Her previous three, which she has described as a “trilogy . . . on the subject of violence and rage,” similarly portray solitary American heroines who have come to far-flung destinations — the Philippines, northernmost Finland, Turkey — in order to heal homegrown trauma. In “The Diver’s Clothes Lie Empty,” the nature of “the horror” that has spurred Vida’s protagonist on her solo Moroccan vacation is revealed to us only gradually.
Twentieth-century novelists from Joseph Conrad to Graham Greene used exotic settings to examine the dark underside of Western imperialism. Vida writes for a world in which there is no more “exotic”: Her Casablanca is one of the nonplaces global capitalism creates, a grid of international hotels, conference centers and chain restaurants, where “everyone is dressed as though going to a business meeting in London or an upscale lunch in New York” and “no one is dressed as though they are in Morocco.” The expensive neighborhood in which the film is being shot is called “California,” and its houses do indeed look like Beverly Hills mansions.

Vida, who lives in the San Francisco Bay Area, is an editor of the cultural review The Believer and a board member of 826 Valencia, the nonprofit center co-founded by her husband, Dave Eggers, to help local children with their writing. Yet for someone whose professional life is dedicated to the creation of community and the transmission of cultural passions, Vida’s fiction exudes a deep loneliness.
This novel’s heroine, whom Vida addresses in the second-person singular as “you,” is a 33-year-old woman from Dellis Beach, Fla., childless and in the process of a painful divorce. She is somebody who has always felt obscurely “mediocre,” poorer, plainer, less effective than those around her. “You attended an expensive all-girls school on scholarship,” where the other mothers seemed to be watching yours disapprovingly; “the grandmothers of your friends didn’t work, had never worked, but your grandmother worked as a cashier at a department store”; “your” twin sister, with whom “you” never managed to share the cozy intimacies of other twins, was prettier than you and more outgoing (“She felt her genes were better than yours”), whereas “your” face is marred by acne scars and you have spent much of your life staring out of windows. Although “you” became an accomplished swimmer and won a diving scholarship to college, there was “a reason why you finally arrived at diving as your competitive sport: With diving your face was virtually unseen.” You married your husband largely because he never looked at you: “You thought that with him you could be invisible, until you realized that wasn’t at all what you wanted.”

While checking in to her hotel — a hotel that is disappointingly drab compared with the sleeker, more luxurious international hotels she passed en route to her own — Vida’s protagonist discovers that the knapsack containing her laptop, passport and wallet has been stolen.
What begins as a nervous tourist’s third-world nightmare, feeding paranoid fantasies that both the hotel staff and the police are “in on the plot,” becomes instead a high-stakes liberation from her sad, tarnished self. At the police station, the police chief triumphantly presents our heroine with a knapsack almost identical to hers, from which he produces “with a snap of his wrist . . . as though he’s a blackjack dealer giving you your last card,” the United States passport of a young woman named Sabine Alyse who looks much like her, but without the acne. Is it only her imagination, or is she being pressured to accept belongings both parties know aren’t hers?
It’s a Faustian moment. The Casablanca police chief is not the only blackjack artist at this table. Vida’s novelistic task is to convince the reader that her “you” wouldn’t do what the reader’s “you” would surely do: i.e., explain politely that this is not your knapsack, and throw yourself on the mercy of the American Embassy’s emergency services.
Instead, from a persuasive combination of jet lag, greed, opportunism and submission (“You’re not sure what will happen if you protest”), the protagonist finds herself signing her name as “Sabine Alyse” to the blood-red-stamped police report. It’s revealing of the demons driving the young woman’s identity fraud that “Sabine’s” first move — before swapping hotels for the more elegant Regency, with its white orchids and deep, plush mocha-colored sofas and piped-in Lauryn Hill music — is to buy with her alter ego’s still uncanceled credit cards a stash of makeup to hide her acne scars.
Vida is adept at subverting all the formulas her novel would seem to be invoking: From helpless victim of a Kafkaesque muddle, her protagonist turns ­consumer-predator, a Bonnie without a Clyde. Yet just when she — and we — imagine that the jig is up, one more gift of an identity upgrade saves our diver’s bacon: The “famous American actress” starring in the film being shot in Casablanca has just lost her stand-in, and “Sabine Alyse” (now posing as “Reeves Conway”) is asked to take her place. Five hundred dollars a day in Moroccan dirhams, free accommodations, a chance to become instant best friends with this charmingly foul-mouthed beauty who, it turns out, needs a stand-in not just for the film shoot but to go backstage after Patti Smith concerts and on dates with unsavory Russian businessmen. Is this a new beginning, we wonder, a true case of “punctuated equilibrium,” or merely a more madcap reprise of our heroine’s lifelong role as “stand-in” to her prettier twin? Is Casablanca really going to be different from Dellis Beach?
Like Claire Messud’s “The Woman Upstairs,” in which a schoolteacher falls under the spell of a glamorous but unscrupulous artist, Vida’s novel portrays with cool wit and suspense the explosive emancipation of a woman who, long accustomed to playing handmaiden to more vivid personalities, is finally empowered to grab some warmth, drama, magic for herself.
THE DIVER’S CLOTHES LIE EMPTY
By Vendela Vida
216 pp. Ecco/HarperCollins Publishers. $25.99.

Phys Ed
Gretchen Reynolds on the science of fitness.
Older athletes can be much younger, physically, than they are in real life, according to a new study of participants in the coming Senior Olympics. The study found that the athletes’ fitness age is typically 20 years or more younger than their chronological age, providing a clear inspiration to the rest of us to get out and start moving more.
I wrote
last year about fitness age
, a concept developed by researchers at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology in Trondheim who had taken note of epidemiological data showing that people with above-average cardiovascular fitness generally had longer life spans than people with lower aerobic fitness. So at any given age, fit people were relatively younger than were people who were out of shape.
But the researchers decided that their insight was not useful unless people could easily determine their fitness age. So using a mobile exercise laboratory, they went out and tested the fitness and health of more than 5,000 Norwegian adults and used the resulting data to create a sophisticated algorithm that could rapidly calculate someone’s aerobic capacity and relative fitness age based on his or her sex, resting heart rate, waist size and exercise routine.
They then set up a beguilingly simple
online calculator
that people could use to determine their fitness age.
When I wrote about the calculator last year, Dr. Pamela Peeke took note. An assistant professor of medicine at the University of Maryland and board member of the foundation that runs the National Senior Games — which are informally known as the Senior Olympics — she is also a competitive triathlete.
And biologically, it seems, she is a spring chicken. When she plugged her personal data into the online fitness calculator, it told her that her fitness age is 36.
Chronologically, she is 61.
Delighted, she wondered whether other older athletes would be similarly youthful. And she had a plan for how to find out. Contacting the scientist who had led the development of the fitness age calculator, Ulrik Wisloff, she suggested that together they study a particular group of older people — the participants in this year’s Senior Olympic Games.
The Senior Olympics are a biennial competition for athletes over 50 and consist of a variety of sports, from track and field and swimming to pickleball. To compete, athletes must first qualify regionally.
More than 4,200 men and women aged from 50 to 100 have qualified for this year’s Games, which begin on Friday in and around Minneapolis-St. Paul, in Minnesota.
Senior Olympians are not professional athletes, but most train frequently, Dr. Peeke knew. They tend to be more physically active than other people of the same chronological age.
To see just how their lifestyle affects their biological age, she and Dr. Wisloff asked all of this year’s Senior Olympic qualifiers to complete the online calculator. They set up a special, dedicated site for the participants, so that their data could be isolated. (The fitness calculator itself was unchanged.)
Virtually all of the participants complied, producing more than 4,200 responses.
The results were impressive. While the athletes’ average chronological age was 68, their average fitness age was 43, a remarkable 25 years less.
“This is a massive difference,” Dr. Wisloff says. “I had expected a big difference,” he continued, “since these people have trained for years. However, I was surprised that it was this big.”
The effect was similar for both male and female athletes, he pointed out. Virtually every athlete, in fact, had a lower fitness age than his or her chronological age.
Dr. Peeke and Dr. Wisloff have not yet determined whether athletes in certain of the sports at the Senior Olympics, particularly endurance events such as distance running and swimming, have a younger fitness age, in general, than athletes participating in less-vigorous sports.
But they plan to parse the data extensively in the coming months to answer that question and to look for other patterns among the Senior Olympians. They expect to publish their findings soon.
Even in advance of that information, though, the takeaway message of the data should be inspiring, said Dr. Peeke, who will be competing in the triathlon event at the Senior Olympics.
“A majority of the athletes at the Senior Games didn’t begin serious training until quite late in life, including me,” she said. “We may have been athletes in high school or college. But then, for most of us, jobs and families and other commitments got in the way, at least for a while.”
Few Senior Olympians returned to or began exercising and training regularly until they were middle-aged or older, she said.
“So you can start any time,” she said. “It’s never too late.”
Qualifying competitions for the 2017
National Senior Games
begin next year.

SHOTS ON THE BRIDGE
Police Violence and Cover-Up in the Wake of Katrina
By Ronnie Greene
240 pp. Beacon, $24.95.
Six days after Hurricane Katrina, a crew of New Orleans police officers open fire on a group of unarmed civilians, killing two. Then, to cover up their crime, they arrest one of the survivors, Lance Madison; produce a gun supposedly confiscated at the scene; and conjure two corroborating witnesses out of thin air (“Lakeisha Smith” and “James Youngman”). If “Shots on the Bridge” were a crime novel, this plot would seem implausible, but these are all established facts painstakingly woven together from interviews, site visits and court records by Greene, an investigative journalist for The Associated Press.
The book opens with the storm gathering strength, as Lance Madison makes the fateful decision to ride it out with his brother Ronald, a disabled 40-year-old with the mind of a child. It seems a sensible and compassionate decision — their family’s inland evacuation space couldn’t take pets, and Ronald’s life revolves around his two dachshunds — but Ronald ends up dead, shot as the brothers try to flee the devastated city on the Danziger Bridge, and Lance is arrested. The narrative ends in the spring of 2015, more anticlimax than cliffhanger, without a resolution of the case against the officers, their convictions vacated, at least for now, and a new trial most likely in the offing.
Too often Greene’s pulp-fiction-style prose (“a city buried in water, panic and death”; “The lies broke open like the levees”) blunts the strength of his material. Oddly, the most haunting question isn’t raised. Had the police pinned the blame on a more typical hurricane victim instead of a middle-class Afro-Asian college graduate whose family could meet his $400,000 bail, hire an attorney and, through Beltway connections, generate a letter to the attorney general of the United States, might the vicious, fictitious New Orleans Police Department story have stuck?
LEFT TO CHANCE
Hurricane Katrina and the Story of Two New Orleans Neighborhoods
By Steve Kroll-Smith, Vern Baxter and Pam Jenkins
210 pp. University of Texas. Cloth, $75; paper, $24.95.
How to analyze the role of social class in the Katrina catastrophe? Taking on this important question, the University of New Orleans sociologists Baxter and Jenkins and their former colleague Kroll-Smith, now of the University of North Carolina, Greensboro, came up with a fine plan: to compare the ordeals of two black neighborhoods, working-class Hollygrove and middle-class Pontchartrain Park.
Down-at-the-heels Hollygrove sprang up after World War I. Crisscrossed by highways, train tracks and canals, it was simply what was left after the urban planners finished drawing their maps. In contrast, Pontchartrain Park, a cynical product of the late Jim Crow-era “separate but equal” doctrine, was built as a planned community of 1,000 single-family homes arrayed around a blacks-only golf course. Socioeconomically disparate but similarly below sea level, both Hollygrove and Pontchartrain Park took on several feet of water when the levees broke.

The authors conducted 68 lengthy interviews with survivors from the two neighborhoods, running through their experiences from disaster preparation to rebuilding. But eventually Kroll-Smith, Baxter and Jenkins found themselves at a loss. So many aspects of the Katrina ordeal — where outside New Orleans one happened to have family and friends; which FEMA official answered the phone; whether a particular local bureaucrat was better swayed by a calm request or an emotional outburst — seemed, as their title puts it, left to chance. Moreover, levels of hardship couldn’t always be predicted by socioeconomic status: “Joseph Pratt, a lifelong resident of Hollygrove and jack-of-all-trades . . . hot-wired a truck, siphoned gas and drove himself and others to Baton Rouge and out of harm’s way. These are working-class skills.” In an emergency, handyman training may prove more useful than a college degree, but when a hurricane is approaching isn’t it even better to have the middle-class prerogative of owning a reliable car? “We don’t have a theory about their stories,” the authors confess. “Our goal in this book is to create a little disorder of our own.”
IS THIS AMERICA?
Katrina as Cultural Trauma
By Ron Eyerman
183 pp. University of Texas. Cloth, $75; paper, $24.95.
How did Katrina go from being “a traditional rough-weather story, something for the Weather Channel,” to a news event that upended America’s very sense of itself? That transformation is carefully retraced by Eyerman, a professor of sociology at Yale. Recounting how the story developed day by day in the major print and broadcast media, he reminds readers that when the storm first made landfall the coverage emphasized Mother Nature as an equal-opportunity destroyer. Reporters on the Mississippi Gulf Coast noted that beachfront mansions and scraggly trailer parks were leveled with the same abandon, but after the levees failed the narrative began to change as a glaring if uncomfortable fact was acknowledged: Even for a city as black and as poor as New Orleans, the hardest-hit hurricane victims were disproportionately black and poor.
With the Bush administration doing a “heck of a job,” the narrative turned political (the emperor has no clothes) and then geopolitical (the empire has no clothes) as the United States accepted emergency aid from countries like Mexico, Uganda and Zimbabwe. By calling into question America’s self-image as a prosperous, high-functioning first-world superpower, Eyerman notes, “Katrina delivered a staggering blow to the myth of American exceptionalism.” By the end, this was a story of lost innocence and national trauma, an event more often compared to the 9/11 terrorist attacks than to other natural disasters.
Hovering over his material in the sweet spot between engagement and detachment, Eyerman reconstructs the media coverage even as he critiques it. To him, the nation’s shock after Katrina betrays not our innocence but our ignorance: “That the majority of those left behind with no means to escape an emergency in a large Southern city would be black and poor would surprise no one with any interest at all in the history of the United States.”

To the Editor:
Re “
Shoot First, and He’ll Answer Questions
” (front page, Aug. 2), about William J. Lewinski, a psychologist who has been called as an expert witness to help “justify countless shootings” by police officers and whose company “has trained thousands of police officers on how to think differently about police shootings that might appear excessive”:
Dr. Lewinski’s strategy of reflexively defending police use of deadly force in every encounter, regardless of other concerns, relies on a blind trust in law enforcement and ignores the brutal reality that people of color disproportionately face of death at the hands of the police. It is time for all of us to say this is not justice, but a justification for sanctioned murder.
DON BULLICK
San Francisco
To the Editor:
William J. Lewinski may be correct about some things, but his mission is misguided. The question is not how to guarantee police officers’ safety.
Most people I know believe that officers should be certain of the threat before responding with deadly force. Stated simply, we honor and respect police officers because we think they are willing to take a bullet rather than kill an innocent person (like us). Police officers who think differently should get into another, safer line of work.
Until we expose and root out the bad training and flawed thinking that allow or even lead officers to place their own safety above that of ordinary citizens, we will not change the epidemic of questionable police shootings.
RICHARD W. POETON
Bennington, Vt.
To the Editor:
You report that William J. Lewinski has become “a hero to many officers who feel that politics, not science or safety, drives police policy.” These officers, you say, complain about rules requiring them “to consider less lethal options such as pepper spray, stun guns and beanbag guns” before resorting to firearms, rules that you quote Les Robbins, the executive director of the
Association for Los Angeles Deputy Sheriffs
, as saying “have come about because of political pressure.”
I am all for science and safety, but police officers are ultimately accountable to the public. We pay them to protect us and make us safer. So yes, like it or not, politics
should
drive police policy. The “political pressure” exists for a good reason. It is the way our society is supposed to work.
JOHN MASON
Westport, Conn.
To the Editor:
I am a retired deputy sheriff, having worked in Seattle and Los Angeles. And I have found that while most shootings involving officers are, indeed, justified, sometimes even when the suspect is, ultimately, found to have been unarmed, others are what we refer to as “bad shoots.”
During my career, I was involved in only one shooting; it was completely justified, as the suspect was trying to run me down with his stolen vehicle. According to William J. Lewinski’s way of thinking, I would have been justified on several other occasions had I shot civilians, though such shootings would have proved to be not at all justified in my mind as a professional.

I was a training officer and field supervisor, and I emphasized “officer safety” tactics. And though I’m loath to second-guess a fellow officer, some are simply too fearful to be doing the job properly. Ours is a dangerous profession, fraught with the need to make split-second decisions. But we must not condone a “shoot first, ask questions later” mentality.

Santa Fe, N.M.
To the Editor:
William J. Lewinski says he did not submit and publish his research findings on which he bases his testimony and teaching in a scientific journal but published in a police magazine because he wanted to reach that target audience.
To assume that his findings would have been successfully published in a peer-reviewed academic journal may be wishful thinking. But for Dr. Lewinski to cite his experimental work in court to explain police shootings of unarmed suspects is more problematic.
Certainly, he knows that scientific findings (even his own) are not accepted (scientifically speaking) until they are independently verified (replicated and published with peer review). One would hope that prosecutors, judges and juries would know this, too.
ALAN W. LANGER
Glen Allen, Va.
The writer is a retired professor of psychology at Syracuse University who has published in, and done peer reviews for, scientific journals.
To the Editor:
Your news article starts with a story about William J. Lewinski testifying for a white police officer who had told a black motorist to take his hand out of his pocket and then shot and killed the man when he began to do so. Dr. Lewinski, you say, “explained that the officer had no choice but to act.” But if the police officer was going to shoot the driver if he took his hand out of his pocket, should the officer not have told the driver to keep his hand where it was?
JOY VAN KLEEF
Toronto

WASHINGTON — ARE women necessary?
Not with Ava around.
Even without hair on her head or flesh on her legs, Ava has enough allure and cunning to become a classic film noir robot vixen.
Despite being a plastic and mesh gizmo locked in a glass cell, she can enmesh men with frightening ease.
Ava is the appealing heroine, or apocalyptic villainess, of “Ex Machina,” a stylish sci-fi thriller set in the near future, written and directed by Alex Garland, a 44-year-old Brit who wrote the 2002 zombie hit “28 Days Later.”
Critics are divided over whether “Ex Machina” is a feminist fable or misogynistic nightmare. Like Quentin Tarantino with violence, Garland has it both ways: He offers a mocking meditation on the male obsession with man-pleasing female sex robots while showing off an array of man-pleasing female sex robots.
Ava, played with a delicate edge by the Swedish actress and dancer Alicia Vikander, is far more than a “basic pleasure model,” as some female replicants in “Blade Runner” are known. She has wiles that are a lot more potent than the weaponized breasts of Austin Powers’s fembots.
Her Dr. Frankenstein is an abrasive Steve Jobs-type named Nathan, played by a hypnotic Oscar Isaac.
“Is it strange to have made something that hates you?” Ava icily asks Nathan.
Nathan has a peach-fuzz coder in his firm, Caleb, fly to his hideaway in Alaska to test whether the curvy artificial-intelligence machine can outwit a nerdy human. It quickly becomes clear that Caleb, in the great film noir tradition of love-struck saps, is going to have a tough time with this silicon femme fatale. Nathan devilishly confides that Ava has a sexual “opening with a concentration of sensors” and admits that he modeled her appearance on Caleb’s online porn history.
Garland has said that it’s “tricky” to assign gender to robots because it raises questions about whether sexuality is a component of consciousness, and he has called Ava’s femininity purely external. But, given how much her looks and charms drive the movie, he told me that it feels “oddly wrong” to call Ava “it.”
Indeed, he confesses to having “a sort of crush” on his creation, and answers “No” a bit too quickly when I ask whether we should assume that Nathan, who lives alone in his glass house with his android Galateas, has had sex with Ava.
Does that notion make him jealous?
“Maybe,” he concedes. “That’s not an unreasonable thing to say.”
Asked if he would want a sex robot, the married father of two replies: “Could I imagine falling in love with a robot that was sentient and attractive to me? Well, sure, I could. But do I want a complicated version of a vibrator? No, I don’t. Some people might. I’m not judgmental about it.”
I ask if the movie will enhance the fear of some women that guys are more into the porn stars on their phones than the girls on their arms.
“The thing we desire and think we can’t have we can now shape exactly to the specification of how we want it,” he says. “There’s something incredibly scary about how unstoppable it feels.”

“Ex Machina” arrives in theaters amid a raft of stories about the swift advance in robotics, with everything from
investment-banker bots that make stock picks
to blueprints for
spider-shaped bots that can potentially spy or assassinate
.
Some visionaries — Stephen Hawking, Elon Musk and Steve Wozniak —
warn that humans will be superseded by robots
, who will soon be smart enough to redesign themselves to become exponentially smarter.
“Will we be the family pets?”
Wozniak fretted to The Australian Financial Review
.
Garland is not alarmed because he views robot superiority as inevitable. He suggests that we view androids not as our competitors but as our progeny — or “mind children,” as robotics expert Hans Moravec, who believes they will be their own species, calls them.
Garland talks about all the things, including government programs, that would run more smoothly with an A.I. in charge. Can he can envision an A.I. president, even more sleek and less emotive than the one we have now?
“There could be an A.I. president; there could,” he replies.
Talking about Ava being programmed to Caleb’s porn preferences, I tell Garland that this is a scary scene, given all the Julian Assanges of the world who are eager to spill our most private exchanges. He says he’s more worried about surreptitious humans than sentient robots and noted that Nathan’s “dude-bro” speak is a metaphor for how tech companies lure us into divulging our lives.
“It’s like your hipster best friend that you aspire to, which is often how these companies market themselves,” he says. “They’re your mate, your buddy. ‘Now let’s go to this club; let’s hang out.’ And a sense that the familiarity of that is just pulling your attention away from the fact that they’re going through your address book and recording everything in there. And every now and then, pulling a dollar bill out of your wallet and going, ‘Dude, hey.’ ”
As we part, I ask Garland what will end humanity first, zombies or robots?
“Neither,” he says. “We will. We’re going to manage that perfectly without any help from zombies or robots.”

Batteries and chargers and GPS. Snacks and water and sensible shoes. And an awful lot of patience.
Such are the daily necessities of covering a prison break, as I’ve discovered over the last week or so since an otherwise normal early June weekend was interrupted by news of two murderers pulling an old-school breakout from a maximum-security prison high in the Adirondacks.
The prison’s location, Dannemora, N.Y., was unknown to me before Saturday, June 6, but fast became my summer home as the escapees, Richard Matt, 48, and David Sweat, 35, continued to elude authorities.
Finding and getting to the action is the first step in any coverage, and has been easy enough in this case from my home in Albany, about 170 miles south of the prison. But with the search area fluid and expanding and prone to rumor — “They’re in Willsboro!,” “They’re in Philadelphia!,” “They’re right behind you!” — an ability to pivot fast and change direction has also been key. I’ve kept GoogleMaps and MapQuest up and running on my laptop in the passenger seat just in case there is a solid sighting or a capture, neither of which has been in the offing yet.
The chase thus far has involved a series of sprints and lulls; the hunt initially lurched in several directions and then settled into a painstaking process of “grid” searches near the prison as hundreds of officers walked miles of territory looking for clues.
But because the search area is big — about five square miles and growing — reporters have often been in motion; circling the perimeter, sometimes literally chasing helicopters, other times pulling off the road to watch police go door-to-door or search the myriad barns, sheds and vehicles that dot properties. More surreal, and more chilling, frankly, have been the moments when a pack of searchers, often camouflaged suddenly materializes from the woods, carrying Sig Sauer rifles and heavy packs. But no escapees.
There’s been a media crush over the last week, though the number dwindled over the weekend. It’s been a very collegial bunch – often sharing information they’ve heard or leftovers from lunch – and also almost inescapable: Hotels in nearby Plattsburgh (there’s nowhere to stay in tiny Dannemora) quickly filled up with people from media and law enforcement, many of whom seemingly awaken before dawn. (I noted that parking lots that were full at night were usually half-empty by the time I headed out to the scene each morning at 7 a.m. or so.) Hotel bars have been a useful place to catch up on the latest, and hear a few tipsy tips.
We’ve had a series of great reporters up here – Rick Rojas and Sarah Maslin Nir, among them – and great staff in New York. In my case, I have usually been traveling alone but talking or texting with colleagues constantly. My car has been the office, the passenger seat my desk. And like my desk in Albany, it is an embarrassing mess, an unruly salvage yard of used coffee cups and diet soda bottles, notepads and napkins, copies of the competition’s work and cords of various lengths and uses.
Without sounding like too much of a throwback – I remember rotary phones but did not personally know Alexander Graham Bell – there are limits to technology, particularly when one is in a remote location with sketchy cell service a scarcity of electrical outlets near its wooded areas. So actual maps, made of actual paper, have also come in handy on a couple of occasions. The navigation has been used in trips from Dannemora, high in the Adirondacks, to the edges of Lake Champlain, where searchers hunted outside Willsboro, N.Y., and across all manner of byway between: country roads, rural cut-throughs, and an occasional dirt road. Sometimes it is easier to pull out a map than to pull out the laptop and hope the Wi-Fi is working.
While live tweeting an ongoing search was exciting for me (and for readers, I hope), keeping the information coming can result in premature graying. I’m not a photographer, but have felt that photos of the continuing search might be interesting to readers. But sending a constant stream of snapshots eats power, and I’ve cursed the fading battery on my smartphone on several occasions, and thanked higher powers for the invention of the car charger on several others. My digital tape recorder has also had a workout, both in capturing the comments of state officials and periodically noting my own thoughts as I’ve worked the story. (“Must buy more batteries for tape recorder,” has been a common one.)
The conditions of the search – conducted in a beating, river-swelling rain on several occasions – have also been tough on equipment. My binoculars — which came in handy while watching search teams comb distant fields outside Willsboro — are toast, having been flooded with water and now fogged. My digital camera escaped, but my black dress shoes – a poor choice of footwear, no doubt — are now beaten-down loafers. My jeans are still a couple cycles away from being dry.
I have always snickered at the wind blazers and rain coats television reporters wear in live shots on hurricane stories. But after days of what have seemed like endless rain, I now understand the errors and arrogance of my ways. Likewise, I’ve often tsk-tsked about the giant news crews’ vans and all the equipment therein, but I’ve found out that you can never have enough pads, pens, or granola bars. Stock up; they keep.
The intensity of the search – and media attention – has been its own challenge. While The Times and other venues have had big crews of reporters on the story, the rumor mill can be awfully distracting, as snippets told to one journalist often spread through the herd. It’s the same with various tweets and online theories: Some locals told me they avoid “Falsebook” after a big number of supposed sightings and other digital detritus — including a rogue posting last week that one of the escapees was dead — have cropped up on Facebook.
Sorting through bad information is an inexact science, but the urge to compete and break news tests your news judgment.
Perhaps the most critical tool in a simmering story like this is one the state troopers and other law enforcement officials have been pleading with local residents to employ: patience. Maybe because of police procedural dramas which wrap up in an hour, and partly perhaps because of the anxiety caused by Mr. Matt and Mr. Sweat being on the loose, it’s easy to feel frustrated by the pace of the investigation and subsequent news stories about the manhunt.
More than 800 officers from various local, state and federal agencies want this to be over, too. The search has presented a serious challenge under difficult circumstances, and the officers searching for the escaped convicts are under close media scrutiny.
I’ve reminded myself to enjoy the long days and nights in the Plattsburgh hotel. Journalism is sometimes a tough occupation — though not hunting-killers tough, of course — subject to long hours, stress, competition and occasional beat-downs.
As the search continues and the dragnet remains empty, I’m heading back to Albany, leaving the story in the good hands of my colleagues Michael Winerip, Vivian Yee, Michael Schwirtz and Rick Rojas, who has been working on the story since Day 1.
A story like the Dannemora search — with  all its mystery and drama — makes me happy to do the work I do. When my jeans dry, I’ll be happier still.

“He was beating me upside the head,” Floyd Dent, a 57-year-old longtime autoworker told a gaggle of reporters last week,
according to The Detroit Free Press
. “I was trying to protect my face with my right arm. I heard one of them say, ‘Tase the M...F.’ ”
Dent was describing what he experienced in a horrifically violent dashboard camera video that shows Inkster, Mich., police officers pulling him over, dragging him from his car, punching him 16 times in the head and tasing him three times, while he lay bloody and struggling on the ground, before arresting him.
According to the
website for a local NBC News affiliate
: “Police said they first saw Dent’s car through binoculars while watching an area known to have drug activity. They followed Dent’s car and said he didn’t make a complete stop at a stop sign. Police said that when they turned on their flashing lights, Dent didn’t immediately pull over.”
Furthermore: “Police said they ordered Dent to put his hands up, but they could only see one. Police said Dent yelled ‘I’ll kill you’ at the officers. Dent’s attorney, Greg Rohl, said there’s no audio of the alleged threat.”
Finally: “Police said Dent refused to put his hands behind his back. Dent said he thought he was being choked to death and tried to pull the officers’ arms away from his throat. One of the officers said Dent bit him on the arm, and that’s why he started punching Dent. Police said the force was needed to restrain Dent. The officer who said he was bit did not seek medical attention or photograph the bite marks.”
According to The Free Press, “Police initially charged him with assault, resisting arrest and possession of cocaine, insisting they found cocaine beneath the passenger seat of his Cadillac. Dent says police planted the drugs at the time of his arrest. An Inkster district court judge, after reviewing the tape, tossed the assault and resisting charges, but Dent faces an April 1 hearing on the drug charge.”
Dent’s lawyer says the drugs were planted by the officer who punched him, William Melendez. And there is video that the lawyer claims backs up the allegation. As a reporter at the local NBC News affiliate
describes it
: “In the video, the officer seen throwing the punches, William Melendez, is seen pulling something from his pocket that looks like a plastic baggy with something inside it. Melendez testified in court police found a baggy of crack cocaine under the passenger seat of Dent’s car.”
It should be noted that, according to the local NBC News affiliate website, Dent said a blood test showed no drugs in his system.
It should also be noted that,
according to The Free Press
, Melendez, who federal investigators in 2003 said “was known on the street as ‘Robocop,’ ” “has been involved in 12 lawsuits related to his conduct as an officer over the years, including similar allegations in a civil rights suit now pending in federal court.”
Those lawsuits allege, “among other things, that he planted evidence, assaulted people in their homes, fabricated police reports and wrongly arrested people.”

Videos like the Dent footage further the perception, especially among African-Americans, that the police are more likely to use force — specifically deadly force — against blacks than whites.
A December
CBS News poll
found that 84 percent of blacks and 33 percent of whites believe that the police in most communities are more likely to use deadly force against blacks. Just 2 percent of whites, and 0 percent of blacks, believe the police are more likely to use such force against whites.
(Fifty-seven percent of whites and 10 percent of blacks said they thought race did not affect the use of deadly force.)
And it is important to register where the most recent cases are centered.
As Isabel Wilkerson, author of the monumental book “The Warmth of Other Suns,” put it in a January New York Times essay titled “When Will the North Face Its Racism?”: “High-profile cases of police brutality have recently come to be associated with the North rather than the South. And it is in the South that two recent cases of police shootings of unarmed black people resulted in more vigorous prosecution.”
She concluded: “If the events of the last year have taught us anything, it is that, as much progress has been made over the generations, the challenges of color and tribe were not locked away in another century or confined to a single region but persist as a national problem and require the commitment of the entire nation to resolve.”
So much about Dent’s case is troublesome, and so he has become the latest touchstone in our coalescing conversation about the intersection of police forces and communities of color, particularly in the parts of this country that African-Americans fled to in search of a better life.

Though it is nothing she would have wished for, in a relatively short time
Nancy Borowick
became an expert in photographing death.
First it was her father, Howie, 58, who died from pancreatic cancer weeks after her photo essay on his illness was
published in The Times
in late 2013. Almost a year to the day after his death, her mother, Laurel, 59, died last Dec. 6 after a 20-year battle with breast cancer. Ms. Borowick now has a second set of images that tell her mother’s story.
A Look Back on Lens
Nancy Borowick photographed both her parents receiving cancer treatment in 2013 as she planned for her wedding. She shared her photos and story with Lens.
View More»
That wasn’t the original plan. Ms. Borowick, 29, had started photographing her mother in 2009 for a class project at the International Center of Photography. The idea was to chronicle her fight against a recurrence of breast cancer.
Ms. Borowick had wanted to learn more about the treatment process, and trailing her mother would let them spend more time together. The daughter didn’t know a lot about cancer then. She had expected to tell a hopeful story — her mother, who exercised faithfully and ate right, had beaten cancer in the 1990s and had been healthy for more than a decade.
Then, in December 2013, came the unexpected twist: her father’s pancreatic cancer, with a life span that was counted in months rather than years.
That first essay was largely a love story, her parents going through treatment together, taking chemotherapy side-by-side, celebrating the good days, surviving the bad, together. That spring there was another twist, Nancy’s decision to marry in time for her parents to walk her down the aisle, more photos about love.
This second photo essay is all about death.
“We are scared of death and I think that is in large part because we hide it away, out of sight and avoid it until we have to,” she wrote.
“I’ve gained a lot of perspective since my father died and no moment was wasted this past year with my mother.”
There are other reasons the photos of her father’s death have such a different feel from the photos of her mother’s. Howie Borowick was a public person, a highly successful trial lawyer, so good at what he did that companies sometimes would settle out of court rather than face him in court. He was outgoing, fast to make friends, open with strangers, terrible at keeping secrets, funny in a noisy way, a person who loved to preen and never tired of his own stories.
Laurel Borowick was a private person, also a lawyer, but she had given up the law to raise their three children. She was quieter, thoughtful, introspective, observant, amusing, nurturing, involved in her community and very well read. Howie was a doer. Laurel was an intellectual in the sense that ideas dominated her thinking. She made a list of books she wanted to read before she died. And as anyone who had been married to Howie Borowick for 34 years would have to be, she was an excellent listener, much to the benefit of her children.
Laurel Borowick was the kind of person who didn’t want to impose on people. Howie was sure he wasn’t.
It is not a coincidence that many of the photos of Laurel are taken in their home and are about family. The home she had created for them was her masterwork.
This photo essay is a series of progressions toward death, taken by a photographer who knew what was coming.
First, the machinery that forestalls death. When the oxygen tank arrived, they didn’t think Laurel needed it yet, but soon it was ever-present. “With a twenty-five-foot tube attached, the machine, which she playfully called WALL-E after the cartoon character, rolled along behind her as she went from room to room, slowly and cautiously,” Nancy wrote.
When she could no longer do aerobics, Laurel still had grocery shopping. Then she couldn’t shop, but could read and watch television. She couldn’t concentrate enough to read, but could still listen to people read to her and to music.
“She lost her ability to communicate,” Nancy said. “First it was speech, then nodding, until there was no sign other than the occasional grimace of pain.”
Laurel went silent but was present. And finally, that great mystery of life, the soul that makes us human, disappeared — rises to heaven, a religious person might say — and there is only stillness.

The Supreme Court is hearing two blockbuster cases this term — one on Obamacare, one on same-sex marriage — and it’s easy to think of both of them on a simple right-left spectrum. Many Democrats argue that middle-class households should be allowed to keep their health insurance subsidies and that same-sex couples should be allowed to marry in all 50 states. Many Republicans take the opposite stances.
But the liberal-conservative filter isn’t the only way to think about the two cases. They also occupy different pieces of political territory. On one of those pieces of territory, the left is winning. On the other, the right is.
The health care case — the subject of arguments before the justices this week — is primarily part of the economic debate. Although it’s focused on only one sector, the law is
the most aggressive attack
that the federal government has launched against inequality since inequality began rising four decades ago. It taxes the affluent (and corporations, which are disproportionately owned by the affluent) in order to subsidize health insurance for middle-class and poor households that lack it. If you sometimes wonder why the law has generated such political heat, that fact is the main reason.
As significant as the health law may be, it doesn’t change the reality that the political left is largely losing the battle against inequality. (There is also
a nascent movement
to fight inequality on the right, but it doesn’t yet have much influence on Republican policies.) After-tax income for most American households has risen
only modestly
in the last few decades. It has soared for most wealthy households.
The marriage case, on the other hand, is fundamentally a case about rights and freedom — and on that ground, the left is winning the political war in a rout. A national right to same-sex marriage was unthinkable just a decade ago. It now looks inevitable. Blatant discrimination on the basis of race, religion or sex, similarly, has become far less common in the span of many Americans’ lives.
There are caveats, to be sure. The Justice Department’s report on Ferguson, Mo., this week made clear that black Americans often lack basic rights — like freedom from unjust arrest — that white Americans take for granted. But there is no credible argument that racism is worse than it was 50 years ago. When President Obama speaks at
an anniversary ceremony
for the Selma, Ala., march that took place 50 years ago this Saturday, he will probably point out that happy reality.
The broad point is that the country continues to follow its basic historical arc on civil rights: They expand. African-Americans shed the shackles of slavery and ultimately win the right to vote. Women win the right to vote. Italians, Jews, Latinos, the Irish, the Chinese and other Asians are able to hold jobs they once could not. (
Not so many decades ago
, some editors at The New York Times tried to play down the Jewishness of reporters’ names in bylines.) The progress is uneven — and hard-won, as the surviving Selma marchers know well — but it is undeniable.
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
Economic matters are different: There is no reason to assume that the rise in inequality will reverse or that middle-class living standards will rise at a healthy rate in coming decades. The history of civil rights in the United States is indeed a march, with a clear direction. The history of broad-based prosperity is more complicated. When economic growth is rapid, as it was in the decades just after World War II and in the late 1990s, everyone tends to be benefit. When growth is slower, as it has been for most of the last several decades, nothing guarantees middle-class prosperity. It depends on a series of choices that society makes, on education, tax policy and, yes, health care policy.
Without question, the same-sex-marriage case is a landmark. It could be the Brown v. Board of Education for gay rights — and could change daily life for many couples. But regardless of how the Supreme Court rules this time, same-sex marriage is likely to be the law of the land within relatively short order. Just look at public opinion among people under the age 40. Many of them consider same-sex marriage to be roughly as bizarre as Jewish bylines on the front page of The New York Times.
The fate of health insurance for about seven million people — the stakes in the health care case — is not on such solid historical footing. After all, various presidents, including Harry Truman, Richard Nixon and Bill Clinton, have failed to solve the health insurance problem. Meanwhile, every president of the last 40 years has failed to reverse the rise of inequality. If the Supreme Court effectively cancels the tax breaks and health insurance expansion
for millions of people
, those policies won’t inevitably rise again.
For anyone watching the court this spring, the health care case certainly lacks the historical sweep of the marriage case. The health care case is a technical one dealing with the interpretation of a federal statute. The marriage case is about civil rights. But in terms of their long-term effects on American society, the more technical case may well be the more important.

MEMPHIS —  Fans who arrived at FedEx Forum on Monday night discovered more than 18,000 yellow towels draping every seat. Popularly known as Growl Towels, they featured the phrase “Believe Memphis” in sharply angled cursive.
Sure enough, the scene was festive when the Grizzlies took the court for warm-ups before facing the Golden State Warriors in Game 4 of their Western Conference semifinal series. And then the game actually started, and all that belief turned to frustration and then to anger and finally to muted disappointment.
With their 101-84 victory, the Warriors edged back from the brink of disaster, evening the series at two games apiece. In the process, they unearthed their high-octane offense while figuring out a few ways to slow the Grizzlies.
Stephen Curry collected 33 points, 8 rebounds and 5 assists as the Warriors connected on 14 3-pointers and led by as many as 26. Marc Gasol finished with 19 points and 10 rebounds for the Grizzlies, who shot 37.5 percent from the field and 22.2 percent from 3-point range.
Game 5 is scheduled for Wednesday night in Oakland, Calif.
A star-studded crowd included Gov. Bill Haslam of Tennessee and Tom Izzo, the men’s basketball coach at Michigan State. Izzo watched as two of his former players, Zach Randolph of the Grizzlies and Draymond Green of the Warriors, clashed repeatedly in the paint. Green, booed every time he touched the ball, had 16 points and 10 rebounds.
Before the game, Warriors Coach Steve Kerr described his team’s precarious situation as a “moment of truth.” The Warriors did not face much adversity during the regular season, and Kerr decided to vary his players’ routine ahead of Game 4.
On Sunday, the Warriors gathered to watch the film of their Game 3. All of it. Every possession. Every missed shot. Every turnover. The Warriors typically review isolated clips from the previous game, Kerr said. But this was the first time all season they watched the entire thing.
“It was important to see the rhythm of the game,” Kerr said.
At the same time, Kerr knew he needed to make adjustments of his own. One of them involved concocting a plan to slow the Grizzlies’ Tony Allen, who had created so much havoc through the first three games of the series, particularly on defense.
Kerr’s plan became clear moments after the tip, when Andrew Bogut, the Warriors’ 7-foot center, defended Allen on the Grizzlies’ opening possession — except Bogut did not really defend Allen. Instead, Bogut planted himself in the paint and dared Allen to shoot from the perimeter.
Allen long ago established himself as one of the league’s premier wing defenders, but his jump shot has more moving parts than a lawn mower, and he missed his first three 3-point attempts. After the Warriors seized an early 14-9 lead, the Grizzlies called for a timeout, but the tenor of the game had already been established.
Curry made a 3-pointer in the closing moments of the first quarter for a 28-20 lead. He flexed at his teammates on the bench after dunking for a 47-33 lead. And when defenders overplayed him, he dumped the ball to teammates. The Warriors went ahead by 61-44 before halftime, and the Grizzlies never threatened.

To the Editor:
David Greenberg’s
review
of “One Man Against the World,” by Tim Weiner, and “Being Nixon,” by Evan Thomas (July 19), is insightful, but I would question two points he made.
The constitutional problem with the secret bombing in 1969 was not that Cambodia was a neutral country but that the president undertook it secretly and had records falsified in order to keep it secret from Congress, senior military leaders and the American people (the North Vietnamese Army and the people of Cambodia certainly knew about it).
In May 1970, as part of the 25th Infantry Division, I participated in the invasion of Cambodia. As with any invasion, this operation was carefully planned in advance. It certainly was not “hot pursuit” of an enemy.
JAMES P. PFIFFNER
BURKE, VA.

To the Editor:
David Greenberg has turned out an excellent, perceptive review, but neither he nor Weiner nor Thomas deals with our 37th president’s religion — and the “why” of that omission is intriguing. ‘The End of Plenty’
To the Editor:
While I appreciate
Raj Patel’s review
of my book, “The End of Plenty: The Race to Feed a Crowded World” (July 26), a few of his statements suggest he merely skimmed his copy instead of reading it through. First, he quotes my brief description of the green revolution from the introduction (Page 5) and concludes it “isn’t quite right.” To correct this presumed error, Patel quotes William Gaud, the head of U.S.A.I.D. in 1968, who is credited with naming the new type of agriculture developed by Norman Borlaug and colleagues in the 1950s and 1960s, and then describes its Cold War roots as if I had ignored them. In fact, I quote Gaud in full on Page 72 (with a footnote linking to his entire speech) in the midst of a 20-page chapter describing in depth the Cold War history and political context behind the greatest increase in food production the world has ever seen.
Patel’s desire for more on Malthus, women’s empowerment and “immoderate” responses to the looming food crisis is also puzzling. Two of 14 chapters are devoted to Malthus; one covers family planning and the demographic transition, and fully half of the 408-page book focuses on both practical and radical solutions to the most daunting challenge we have ever faced. These include a “pink revolution” for women that begins with free universal education through high school for girls, and free family planning services, equal land rights and access to farm credit for all women. I also call for immediate curbs on deforestation and grain-based biofuels, the transition to a low-carbon economy and the wholesale transformation of world agriculture from the source of a third of global carbon emissions to a carbon-sequestering sink covering nearly 40 percent of the planet. Though these may not be the solutions Patel endorses, there is nothing easy, moderate or “Goldilocks” about any of them.

To the Editor:
Thad Ziolkowski’s dismissive tone about all surf writing other than William Finnegan’s in
his review
of “Barbarian Days” (July 19) is disappointing and uninformed. Several beautifully written books about surfing were published both before and after the appearance of Finnegan’s “Playing Doc’s Games” in 1992. Both show that life to be challenging on an existential level, in spite of the Beach Boys’ fantasy world spun in Southern California in the 1960s.
Start with Kem Nunn, whose trilogy of novels are individually and collectively very powerful works. “Tapping the Source,” “The Dogs of Winter” and “Tijuana Straits” all use the California surfing world as backdrop. And “Breath,” by Tim Winton, is another elegantly written novel about the surfing life — in this case, the Australian version. All these novels — and I’m sure there are others — brilliantly evoke the hard and beautiful reality of a life committed to riding waves. For those of you out there who want to explore other works in the surfing vein, try any of these. William Finnegan has written a wonderful book, but whether it is the definitive work on the subject remains to be seen.

SEATTLE

Q
Is running or jogging good or bad for people with mild osteoporosis?
Reader Question • 105 votes
A
“Like so many things in medicine, there is no easy yes or no answer” to that question, said
Dr. Bjoern Buehring
, an assistant professor of medicine and director of the Osteoporosis Clinical Research Program at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
In general, he said, some degree of loading and pounding, such as occurs during running, is healthy for bones. “Whenever a load or force acts on a bone, it deforms the tissue” to some extent, he said. Afterward, the affected bones return to their normal shape and, through a remarkable physiological prescience, recognize that they need to be stronger in order to fully withstand that same force next time. So the body stimulates the production of more bone cells. In that way, running prompts bones to become denser and stronger.
But this process only works if bones can tolerate the original stress without bowing and breaking, Dr. Buehring said. People with mild osteoporosis may have bones that are too brittle to bounce back from the forces applied during running — or their bones may not respond well. In fact, bones from two people with the same measured density can respond quite differently to real-world conditions, such as jogging.
So the best option for someone with a diagnosis such as yours is to consult your doctor about your particular fracture risk. If you have cracked a bone in the recent past and the break was attributed to osteoporosis, he said, your doctor will probably tell you that your fracture risk is high and running is inadvisable.
If, on the other hand, your doctor tells you that your fracture risk appears to be low, “it actually might be important to go jogging,” Dr. Buehring said, “because lower-intensity activities,” such as swimming or strolling, “might not load the bone enough” to stimulate further strengthening.
Start slowly, however, if you are new to jogging, he advises. Add distance or speed gradually, and check with your doctor if aches in your legs linger or intensify.

WASHINGTON —  The most influential
friend-of-the-court brief
in living memory was filed by a group of retired military officers in a 2003 affirmative action case.
When the
case was argued
, the justices echoed the brief’s argument that military preparedness would be threatened if service academies could not ensure a diverse officer corps. Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s
majority opinion
, allowing race-conscious admissions at public universities, quoted at length from the brief.
The law firm that filed the brief, now called Sidley Austin, has filed
a new one
by former military officials in the
same-sex marriage
cases to be heard next week. Their message this time is that the patchwork of marriage laws around the country hurts military families and threatens national security.
Most workers can turn down transfers to states that do not recognize their marriages. Members of the military, who are more than twice as likely to relocate as their employed civilian counterparts, do not have that choice.
Forcing service members to move to places where their marriages will cease to be recognized creates a tension between service oaths and wedding vows that hurts recruitment, retention, morale and readiness, the brief said.
“Those willing to risk their lives for the security of their country should never be forced to risk losing the protections of marriage and the attendant rights of parenthood,” the brief said, “simply because their service obligations require them to move to states that refuse to recognize their marriages.”
A second friend-of-the-court brief
, from groups that support gay members of the military and their families, said the current state of affairs put the military at a disadvantage in competing with the private sector in recruiting and retaining good people.
“No legally married couple would look fondly upon a move from a state where the couple’s marriage is recognized to a state where their marriage is annulled for state law purposes,” said the brief, filed by lawyers at Chadbourne & Parke.
The differing treatment of marriages also damages the core military principle, vital to morale, of equitable treatment of service members, the second brief said.
The interests of military personnel figured in
the Supreme Court’s 2013 decision
to strike down the part of the Defense of Marriage Act that barred the federal government from providing benefits to same-sex couples.
Solicitor General Donald B. Verrilli Jr., the Obama administration’s top appellate lawyer, who urged the justices to strike down the law, began
his argument
with a vivid image. Under the law, he said, “the spouse of a soldier killed in the line of duty cannot receive the dignity and solace of an official notification of next of kin.”
In
his majority opinion
in the case, United States v. Windsor, Justice Anthony M. Kennedy bristled at the unfairness of prohibiting same-sex couples “from being buried together in veterans’ cemeteries.”
Since then, the Obama administration has worked to ease the burdens on same-sex couples in the military. It allows them, for instance, to take leaves to get married in states that permit
same-sex marriages
.

But it has hit a roadblock, one that gay rights groups say the government created.
The law granting veterans’ benefits
determines whether a marriage is valid by considering “the law of the place where the parties resided at the time of the marriage.”
The Department of Veterans Affairs
has interpreted
those words to mean that couples who live in a state that does not allow same-sex marriage and get married in one that does are generally not entitled to benefits like disability compensation, loan guarantees and death benefits.
“It is perverse,” the Chadbourne & Parke brief said, “for the government to grant leave to enable a same-sex couple to travel to a state where they can legally marry, for the government to recognize that marriage as valid for however many more years the service member continues to serve, and then suddenly ignore that marriage as soon as the service member retires and obtains veteran’s status.”
A federal appeals court in Washington is considering
a challenge to that interpretation
, but the
Supreme Court
’s decision in the four same-sex marriage cases to be argued next week, among them Obergefell v. Hodges, No. 14-556, may make the challenge moot.

issues a heat advisory when the combination of heat and humidity makes it feel like it’s at least 95 degrees for two consecutive days, or the temperatures reaches 100 degrees.

usually six days

So far, temperatures in July have been at 76.8 degrees, slightly below average.

“That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.”
Those words were first uttered (though to be repeated endlessly) on this date 46 years ago.
On July 20, 1969, two men — Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin — walked on the moon.
The article
was on the front page of The Times that day, with the headline: “Men Walk on Moon; Astronauts Land on Plain. Collect Rocks, Plant Flag.”
Slightly more poetically, the article continued:
“It was man’s first landing on another world, the realization of centuries of dreams… the most dramatic demonstration of what man can do if he applies his mind and resources with single-minded determination.”
It seemed appropriate to note this anniversary as we celebrate another space-age achievement: Last week’s flyby of Pluto by the NASA New Horizons spacecraft.
Of that outer reach of the heavens,
The Times wrote
, “A world three billion miles away with towering mountains of ice, vast smooth plains and many mysteries yet to be revealed.”

The French filmmaker
Benoît Jacquot
’s “
3 Hearts
” has the incalculable advantage of teaming three of Europe’s most revered actresses,
Charlotte Gainsbourg
,
Chiara Mastroianni
and
Catherine Deneuve
, in a proudly old-fashioned romantic melodrama. Those names alone make it sound delectable, and in its outlines, this quintessential Gallic bodice-ripper might be described as a hybrid of “An Affair to Remember” and the German filmmaker Dominik Graf’s recent “Beloved Sisters.”
But its internal clock is askew and the premise of the movie, which is set in the present, feels musty. The screenplay relies on so many mechanical contrivances to make the story gripping that you can hear the rusty machinery clanking.
Ms. Gainsbourg, a lean, fearless adventurer who has survived several films by the Danish provocateur Lars von Trier, plays Sylvie, and Ms. Mastroianni, whose screen characters tend to be insecure, supersensitive women, is Sophie. These devoted siblings of opposite temperament, unknowingly fall in love with the same man, and the heart of the drama is a guessing game of how and when the truth will come out. Ms. Deneuve, as imperturbable as the
Statue of Liberty
, sails through the movie with her customary composure in the role of their mother.
The screenplay, written by the director with Julien Boivent, has to pull a lot of strings to keep the sisters in the dark about their shared inamorato, Marc (Benoît Poelvoorde), a fussy Parisian tax inspector. Marc is not the dashing prince you might expect these glamorous siblings to fall in love with. Although reasonably presentable, he ranks far below Cary Grant, leading man of “An Affair to Remember,” in suavity and charm, and he lacks the boyish radiance of Florian Stetter, who plays the poet and philosopher Schiller in “Beloved Sisters.” Marc’s relative absence of magnetism leaves a hole in the movie’s center.
The story begins when Marc, during a visit to Valence, the provincial town where the sisters live, misses his train back to Paris and by chance meets Sylvie in a bar. Their attraction is instantaneous, and they spend much of the rest of the evening wandering the streets and eventually agreeing to meet at a designated time at the Tuileries Gardens in Paris.
Because the movie doesn’t give us enough time to get to know this newly besotted couple, vicarious identification is difficult. Sylvie, although married to a man whose work is taking him to the United States, shows up for the rendezvous. But on the way, the anxiety-prone Marc suffers a mild heart attack and arrives late, by which time Sylvie has returned home and decided to accompany her husband to Minneapolis.
This being the age of the cellphone, you inevitably wonder why neither Sylvie nor Marc carried one. The obvious answer is that if they had had them, there wouldn’t be a movie. And because their missed connection doesn’t seem fateful so much as sloppy, your heart doesn’t sink.
Marc, returning later to Valence, soon meets Sophie, an antiques dealer who needs help with an audit. Unaware that he has met Sylvie’s sister, he pursues Sophie and they marry. The film makes it very clear that the quality of his passion for Sophie has little of the erotic intensity of his connection to Sylvie. In the meantime, the sisters communicate via Skype.
This deliberately old-fashioned movie from a director who has acknowledged such Hollywood chestnuts as “Back Street,” “Love Affair” and Douglas Sirk films as influences, plays standard Hollywood tricks to prevent Sophie from discovering Marc’s secret past or Marc from learning that his ex is Sophie’s sister. And as Marc avoids telling Sophie the truth, his cowardice diminishes his character.
Even when Sylvie returns for Sophie’s wedding, the secret isn’t revealed until the very last minute.
“3 Hearts” is rated PG-13 (Parents strongly cautioned). For sexual content, brief nudity and smoking throughout.

Judge
Susan Phillips Read
, one of two Republicans on New York State’s highest court, announced on Tuesday she would resign in August, giving Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo another opportunity to shape the court 16 months earlier than expected.
Having served 12 years on the Court of Appeals, Judge Read would not have been forced to resign until January 2017, when her 14-year term ends, but she informed Chief Judge
Jonathan Lippman
in a brief letter on Tuesday she was stepping down on Aug. 24. “It has been both a privilege and a pleasure,” she wrote.
Judge Lippman said Judge Read, who is 67, had informed him she wanted to spend more time with her husband and family. “She said it’s time to make a change in her life,” he said on Wednesday. “She’s been talking for a while about leaving before the end of her term.”
Judge Read, who was appointed by Gov. George E. Pataki, a Republican,
told the New York Law Journal
she had promised her husband she would leave the court when this year’s term ended. “I just feel a personal need to kind of change up my work environment and my life,” she said.
Her departure leaves Judge
Eugene F. Pigott Jr.
the sole Republican on the seven-member panel. Mr. Cuomo, a Democrat, has been relentless in appointing liberal Democrats to fill open seats, pushing the court steadily to the left. Most recently he named Judge
Eugene M. Fahey
, a former trial lawyer from Buffalo, in January to fill a seat vacated by Judge Robert S. Smith, a Republican known for his expertise in commercial law.
Besides finding a replacement for Judge Read this fall, the governor will have a chance to name his own appointees to fill Judge Pigott’s and Chief Judge Lippman’s positions over the next three years.

A Quiet Chief Conductor
What do you think of Kirill Petrenko?
While he’s not exactly an unknown quantity, the respected, reticent, self-effacing Kirill Petrenko, who was introduced on Monday as the new chief conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic, isn’t very well known in America.
Let Michael Cooper
introduce him
to you. Then read the glowing reviews of a couple of the orchestral dates he’s had in this country, with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra
in 2012
and the Cleveland Orchestra
in 2009
.
Mr. Petrenko is best known as an opera conductor, and he has seen great success since 2013 as the music director of the Bavarian State Opera in Munich. I,
and others
, really admired his muscular, detailed take on Wagner’s “Ring” at the Bayreuth Festival in 2013.
Completing ‘Khovanshchina’
I was fairly blown away by Mr. Petrenko’s conducting of Mussorgsky’s “Khovanschina” at the Metropolitan Opera
in 2012
. It was a very different take (more lyrical, more nuanced) than the scorched-earth approach to the Russian repertory that Valery Gergiev made the norm at the Met over the past 20 years or so.
“Khovanshchina” ends with a mass suicide. Mussorgsky never finished or arranged the opera, and one of Mr. Petrenko’s best interventions was to interpolate the soft, haunting ending composed by Stravinsky, rather than the usual crashing finale by Shostakovich. (Micaela Baranello, a musicologist and a contributor to The New York Times,
gives more details
on the different versions on her fantastic blog.)
Commemorating Gunther Schuller
If we take for granted now that musical genres are collapsible and combinable, it’s in large part because of Gunther Schuller, the composer, teacher and writer who coined the term Third Stream to describe the synthesis of classical and jazz styles. He died Sunday at 89.
Here’s Allan Kozinn’s
obituary
. And here’s video
and a full transcript
of a 2009 conversation with Frank Oteri and Schuller.
Happy Birthday
Magnus Lindberg, the Finnish composer of meaty and fierce orchestral soundscapes, turns 58 on Saturday. Here’s a taste of his “Kraft,” with Alan Gilbert and the New York Philharmonic. (And Mr. Lindberg himself on the fearsome piano part.)
Oppens on the Barge
The pianist Ursula Oppens, a modern-music specialist who makes revealing forays into the classics, is never dull.
On Friday
, in the cozy confines of Bargemusic, she’ll play music by Rzewski, Schubert, Beethoven, Corigliano and Scriabin. Ever heard all of them on a single program? I didn’t think so.
